misfits.thing: Asphalt road with white dashed center lane markings
misfits.where: Center of the image, running from the foreground up to the village in the distance
misfits.why: A paved asphalt road with painted lane markings is a modern feature and does not belong in a village around 1350, which would have had dirt or cobbled tracks.

misfits.thing: Chimney on the thatched roof of the left house
misfits.where: Top left, at the peak of the thatched roof
misfits.why: The stone chimney cap sitting on the roof looks like a later-period feature; around 1350 houses like this typically had smoke escaping through the thatch or a hole rather than a built chimney stack.

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road with white dashed center lane markings
misfits.where: Occupies most of the foreground and curves through the middle of the village street
misfits.why: Asphalt paving and painted lane markings are modern road-building features, not found in a village around 1350, which would have had dirt, cobbled, or gravel tracks.

misfits.thing: Asphalt road surface
misfits.where: Center and right foreground, covering the main street
misfits.why: Dark tarmac paving is a modern road material and did not exist in a 14th-century village, which would have had dirt or cobbled tracks.

misfits.thing: White dashed lane markings
misfits.where: Painted down the middle of the road from foreground to background
misfits.why: Painted traffic lane lines are a modern road feature with no place in a village around 1350.

misfits.thing: Brick chimneys
misfits.where: Top left corner above the thatched roof, and on the right-side cottage roofs
misfits.why: Fired-brick chimney stacks are anachronistic for c. 1350 Bohemian village houses, which would have used open hearths and smoke-hole roofs.

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road with white dashed center lines
misfits.where: Center and right of the image, running through the village street
misfits.why: Modern asphalt paving and painted road markings did not exist around 1350; the village street would be dirt or cobbled.

misfits.thing: Asphalt road surface with painted white dashed and solid lane markings
misfits.where: The whole road running through the center of the image, from the foreground up to the village
misfits.why: Asphalt paving and painted traffic lane markings are modern road infrastructure and did not exist in a Bohemian village around 1350, when roads were dirt or stone tracks.

misfits.thing: Paved asphalt road with white dashed center lane markings
misfits.where: Center and right of the image, running down the middle of the village street
misfits.why: Modern asphalt paving and painted road lane markings did not exist around 1350; the street would be dirt, cobbles, or packed earth.

misfits.thing: Tall pink flowering plant (possibly hollyhock) growing beside the left house
misfits.where: Left side of the image, against the white wall near the wooden fence, around the upper-middle left
misfits.why: Hollyhocks were not common in Europe around 1350; they were cultivated there mainly from the 16th century onward, so this plant may be anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Tall brick chimney stack with smoke on the right-hand thatched cottage
misfits.where: Upper right of the image, on the roof of the cottage at the far right edge, with a grey smoke plume rising into the sky
misfits.why: Peasant cottages around 1350 typically had central hearths with smoke escaping through the thatch or a roof opening; a freestanding chimney stack is more typical of later medieval or early modern construction.

misfits.thing: Modern-style street lamp with an electric-looking glowing bulb on a tall dark metal pole
misfits.where: Right foreground, along the edge of the sidewalk beside the shop front
misfits.why: Streetlamps with bulbs and metal poles are modern; 1st-century Roman streets were lit by oil lamps or torches, not electric-style fixtures.

misfits.thing: White canvas awning with a wooden valance and metal-looking brackets over the shop entrance
misfits.where: Above the shop doorway in the center-right
misfits.why: Retractable fabric awnings with wooden frames like this resemble later shopfront designs; Roman shops used simpler wooden shutters or fixed projecting canopies, so the style looks anachronistic.

misfits.thing: Modern metal street lamp with a glass-look lantern head
misfits.where: Right side of the street, along the building facade, rising from the sidewalk edge
misfits.why: Cast-metal street lamps with enclosed electric-style lantern heads are anachronistic for 1st-century AD Rome, which lit streets with oil lamps or torches.

misfits.thing: Glowing electric-looking light fixture
misfits.where: Top of the metal lamp post on the right
misfits.why: The bright, uniform electric-style lamp does not match the flickering oil or torch illumination of ancient Roman streets.

misfits.thing: Black metal street lamp with a curved arm and glowing bulb
misfits.where: Right side of the image, a tall post rising from the pavement near the amphora and extending up past the upper storey of the building
misfits.why: Its cast-iron or modern styling and electric-looking bulb belong to a later era. 1st-century Roman streets were lit by oil lamps, torches, or lanterns, not fixtures like this.

misfits.thing: Modern metal street lamp with an enclosed light fixture
misfits.where: Right side of the image, along the sidewalk edge next to the shop front
misfits.why: Electric-style street lighting with a metal pole and sealed lamp head does not belong to a 1st-century Roman street, which would have been lit by oil lamps or torches.

misfits.thing: Modern-style street lamp with a metal pole and enclosed lamp fixture
misfits.where: Right side of the image, beside the shop doorway and terracotta amphora
misfits.why: Electric-style street lighting is anachronistic for a 1st century AD Roman street, which would have been lit by oil lamps or torches.

misfits.thing: Modern street lamp with metal pole and dome lantern
misfits.where: Right side of the street, on the sidewalk next to the shop front
misfits.why: Metal lamp post with an electric-style bulb is a modern streetlight design; Roman streets in the 1st century AD were not lit by such fixtures.

misfits.thing: Canvas awning/retractable shade over the shop entrance
misfits.where: Above the shop doorway on the right and the red awning on the left
misfits.why: Retractable fabric awnings on metal or wooden arms resemble later European shopfront designs; this style is anachronistic for a 1st-century Roman shop front.

misfits.thing: Ornate scrolled wrought-iron wall bracket holding the hanging lamp
misfits.where: Upper left, on the wall above the shop awning, around x 60-290, y 195-420
misfits.why: Its decorative scrollwork resembles later medieval or early modern ironwork; Roman 1st-century fittings were usually simpler bronze or iron hardware.

misfits.thing: Glass-enclosed hanging lantern with a metal frame
misfits.where: Upper left, hanging from the scrolled iron bracket beside the shop doorway
misfits.why: Enclosed glass-and-metal lanterns are a later invention. Romans used open terracotta or bronze oil lamps, so this lantern looks medieval or later.

misfits.thing: Ornate scrolled wrought-iron wall bracket
misfits.where: Upper left wall, holding the hanging lantern
misfits.why: The decorative curling iron scrollwork resembles later medieval or Victorian ironwork more than the plainer Roman fittings of the 1st century AD.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a grid of clear glass panes
misfits.where: Right wall, beside the seated woman
misfits.why: Window glass was not in common use in Scandinavian houses around 900; openings were typically shuttered or covered with cloth, hide, or oiled membrane.

misfits.thing: Glazed skylight opening in the roof
misfits.where: Top left, in the roof ridge above the smoke
misfits.why: A glazed roof opening looks like a later architectural feature; Viking-age longhouses used smoke holes or simple unglazed openings.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a grid of glazing bars
misfits.where: Right side of the back wall, above the bench where the family sits
misfits.why: Small, gridded, glazed windows were not used in Viking-age longhouses around 900; openings were typically unglazed or covered with cloth or shutters, so a framed multi-pane window looks like a later European feature.

misfits.thing: Window with a six-pane grid that looks like glazed glass
misfits.where: Right wall, beside the seated woman with the braids
misfits.why: Glass window panes were not used in Viking-age houses around 900; openings were typically unglazed or covered with shutters or cloth.

misfits.thing: Window with a multi-pane grid of glass panes and a white painted frame
misfits.where: Center-right of the back wall, between the two shields, behind the seated family
misfits.why: Glass windows with a modern-looking pane grid and sash frame were not used in Viking-age longhouses around 900; such houses had small openings or shutters rather than glazed windows.

misfits.thing: Window with a multi-pane grid of glass panes
misfits.where: Center-right of the back wall, between the two shields, above the seated figures
misfits.why: Glazed windows with a white-framed muntin grid look like a modern or later medieval design. Around 900 a Scandinavian longhouse would typically have had a simple shuttered opening, not glass panes.

misfits.thing: Multi-pane window with a grid of small panes
misfits.where: Center-right wall, behind the father and children
misfits.why: Divided-pane windows like this resemble later glazed windows; around 900 a Viking house would typically have had a small unglazed opening, not a gridded window.

misfits.thing: Striped, patterned flatweave rug
misfits.where: Bottom right foreground and right edge near the bench
misfits.why: The bold multicolored striped design looks like a later kilim or rug style rather than a ca. 900 Scandinavian textile.

misfits.thing: Husky-like dog held by the girl on the right
misfits.where: Lap of the girl in the blue dress, on the right side of the bench
misfits.why: Its grey-and-white coat, pointed face and build resemble a modern Siberian husky or similar northern breed, which were not bred in Viking Age Scandinavia. Dogs of the period looked more like spitz or hound types.

misfits.thing: Glass skylight with a metal-framed window in the roof
misfits.where: Top center of the ceiling, above the fire pit and the smoke column
misfits.why: Glazed roof skylights with framed panes are a modern construction feature. Viking-age longhouses had no glass and relied on smoke holes or open vents in the roof.

misfits.thing: Rectangular roof opening that may be a glazed skylight
misfits.where: Top-left corner of the ceiling, above the hearth
misfits.why: Its flat, pale-blue panel looks like a glass pane, which would be anachronistic for a c. 900 Viking longhouse, where roof openings were typically plain smoke holes.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket with a molded handle
misfits.where: Right side of the image, beside the man's legs on the dirt yard
misfits.why: Its bright blue molded plastic construction is a modern material and design; 1850s farms would use wood, metal, or woven containers.

misfits.thing: Bright blue bucket with a molded plastic look
misfits.where: Held by the farmer at the right-center of the image, around x 850-1000, y 930-1140
misfits.why: Its bright, uniform blue color and molded appearance look like modern plastic; 1850s farm buckets would typically be wood or galvanized/tin metal.

misfits.thing: Black-and-white border collie lying in the yard
misfits.where: Right edge of the yard, around x 950-1088, y 790-920
misfits.why: The border collie is a breed standardized in the late 1800s and later, so this specific dog type is anachronistic for an 1850s farmyard.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket with a wire handle
misfits.where: Held by the farmer at the right-center of the image, next to his legs
misfits.why: Brightly colored molded plastic was not available in the 1850s; a period bucket would be wood, galvanized or tinned metal, or painted tin.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: On the dirt ground at the right side of the yard, near the middle-right of the image, beside the man's legs
misfits.why: Its molded plastic handle and bright blue colour look like mid-20th-century or modern plastic, which did not exist in an 1850s farmyard, where buckets would be wood, iron, or tin.

misfits.thing: Blue plastic bucket
misfits.where: Lower left of the image, beside the farmer's legs (roughly x 30-210, y 1190-1395)
misfits.why: Brightly colored molded plastic was not available in the 1850s. A farm bucket of that period would be wood, metal, or woven material.

misfits.thing: Bright blue plastic bucket with a molded handle
misfits.where: Center-right of the dirt yard, beside the man and the chickens
misfits.why: Its molded plastic form and saturated blue color look like a modern mass-produced plastic pail, not a wooden or metal container a farmer would have used in the 1850s.

misfits.thing: Tricolor black, white, and tan dog resembling a Bernese Mountain Dog
misfits.where: Lying on the dirt yard at the left edge, near the horse and wagon
misfits.why: This large tricolor breed was not standardized until around 1907, so it does not fit an 1850s farmyard.

misfits.thing: Black-and-white barred hen resembling a Plymouth Rock
misfits.where: Lower left, in front of the rooster
misfits.why: The barred Plymouth Rock breed was developed in the 1860s and 1870s, after the 1850s setting.

misfits.thing: Yellow plastic ear tag on the brown-and-white cow
misfits.where: On the cow's left ear, at the left edge of the image near the fence
misfits.why: Yellow plastic livestock ear tags for identification came into use in the 20th century, so they would not appear on an 1850s farm.

misfits.thing: Black-and-white barred hen (barred Plymouth Rock-type chicken)
misfits.where: Bottom right foreground, center-right of the frame
misfits.why: Its distinct barred plumage resembles a breed that was standardized in the 1860s and later, so it is a possible anachronism for an 1850s farmyard, though the flock as a whole is otherwise period-appropriate.

misfits.thing: Black metal dome pendant lamp with a bare light bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the room
misfits.why: Its modern industrial styling and electric bulb do not fit a medieval monastery scriptorium, which would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Black metal dome pendant lamp with a glowing electric-style bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the room
misfits.why: Its industrial dome shade and electric-looking bulb are modern lighting. A medieval scriptorium would be lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight from the windows.

misfits.thing: Hanging pendant lamp with a glowing electric-style light bulb
misfits.where: Top center of the image, suspended from the ceiling beams above the scriptorium
misfits.why: A metal pendant lamp with an incandescent bulb is a modern lighting fixture; a medieval scriptorium would be lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Black metal pendant lamp with a glowing light bulb hanging from the ceiling
misfits.where: Top center of the image, hanging from the vaulted ceiling above the desks
misfits.why: An electric-style pendant fixture with a bulb does not fit a medieval monastery scriptorium, which would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or torches.

misfits.thing: Electric pendant ceiling lamp with a glowing light bulb
misfits.where: Hanging from the ceiling at the top center of the room
misfits.why: Electric light bulbs are a modern invention and do not belong in a medieval monastery scriptorium, which would be lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight.

misfits.thing: Electric light bulb with metal dome shade
misfits.where: Hanging from the wooden ceiling beams at the top center of the room
misfits.why: An incandescent electric bulb and metal lamp shade are anachronistic for a medieval monastery scriptorium, which would have been lit by candles, oil lamps, or daylight from the windows.

misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong in an undisturbed autumn beech forest floor scene.

misfits.where: Center-right of the foreground, lying on the leaf litter below the mushroom cluster

misfits.thing: clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: center-right foreground, lying on the leaf litter near the bottom right of the mushrooms
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural undisturbed beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: clear plastic water bottle with blue screw cap
misfits.where: lower right of the image, lying on the leaf litter in the foreground
misfits.why: Man-made plastic litter does not belong on a natural autumn beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: large pine cone
misfits.where: lower right of the frame, on the leaf litter beside the mushroom cluster (approx. x 680-1020, y 1200-1470)
misfits.why: Pine cones come from conifers, but the scene shows only broadleaf beech trees, so a pine cone is out of place for a pure beech forest floor.

misfits.thing: Steel electricity pylon with power lines
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the meadow near the treeline
misfits.why: Man-made utility infrastructure that is an intrusion into the pristine alpine meadow nature scene, though it is a present-day object and not from the wrong period.

misfits.thing: Steel electricity pylon with power lines
misfits.where: Right side of the image, rising from the meadow near the center-right and stretching across the sky
misfits.why: Man-made industrial utility infrastructure that clashes with an unspoiled alpine meadow nature scene, though it is a present-day object.

misfits.thing: Corrugated blue metal roof on the storehouse
misfits.where: Top of the mud-brick storehouse on the right, across the whole building
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern roofing material. Ancient Egyptian storehouses had flat or vaulted mud-brick or timber roofs.

misfits.thing: Burlap-like sacks with stitched seams
misfits.where: Stacked on the cart, on the left by the storehouse wall, and on the barge at lower right
misfits.why: They look like modern jute or burlap sacks with sewn seams. Ancient Egyptians stored grain in woven baskets, reed bins, and clay or pottery jars.

misfits.thing: Corrugated grey roofing on the storehouse
misfits.where: Top right, covering the mudbrick storehouse building beside the quay
misfits.why: The ribbed, sheet-metal-looking roof reads as modern corrugated metal. Ancient Egyptian storehouses had flat mudbrick or timber roofs, not corrugated sheeting.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof
misfits.where: Top of the storehouse building on the right side of the image
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern roofing material. Around 1400 BC Egyptian buildings had flat roofs of mud, palm-wood beams and matting, not corrugated metal.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof on the warehouse
misfits.where: Top of the storehouse building, right-center of the image
misfits.why: Corrugated galvanized sheet metal is a modern material; ancient Egyptian storehouses had flat or mudbrick-supported roofs of wood, reed, or mud.

misfits.thing: Metal chain linking the boats to the mooring posts
misfits.where: Between the wooden mooring posts along the quay edge, above the reed boats in the lower-middle and left-center of the image
misfits.why: Metal chain was not available around 1400 BC; mooring would have used rope or plaited fiber lines.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof
misfits.where: Covering the mud-brick warehouse on the right side of the quay, across the top of the building
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern material and did not exist in ancient Egypt around 1400 BC, which used flat mud-brick or palm-beam and reed roofing.

misfits.thing: Corrugated metal roof
misfits.where: Top of the mudbrick storehouse on the right side of the quay
misfits.why: Corrugated sheet metal is a modern material. Ancient Egyptian buildings had flat or gabled roofs of mud, reed, or timber.

misfits.thing: Triangular lateen-style sail on the distant boat
misfits.where: Small sailing boat on the river at the upper left
misfits.why: The triangular lateen sail is associated with later Mediterranean and Arab dhow-type craft. Ancient Egyptian Nile sailing vessels used large square sails.

misfits.thing: Small sailboat with a triangular lateen-style sail on the river
misfits.where: Background, center-left, on the blue river near the far bank
misfits.why: The triangular lateen sail is a later rig than the square sails of the New Kingdom, so this boat looks anachronistic for about 1400 BC.

misfits.thing: Stacked sacks with a coarse woven, burlap-like texture
misfits.where: Right side of the quay, piled beside the storehouse and the men carrying jars
misfits.why: Their texture and stacking look more like modern burlap or jute sacks than the baskets, linen, or pottery containers typical of Egyptian storage at this date.
